Article Title: Saudi OpenAI engineer arrested for planting hidden device to record executive meetings
Article Text:
Saudi OpenAI engineer arrested over hidden recording device in executive conference room

A Saudi national and OpenAI engineer has been arrested by US federal agents and charged with allegedly installing a hidden audio recording device in an executive conference room at the AI company to capture sensitive discussions about its technology, the US Justice Department said Tuesday.The employee, identified as 35-year-old Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested on Friday.The complaint did not name the company, but OpenAI confirmed in a separate statement that it had discovered a “sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices”. The company reported the discovery to the FBI and fired the employee.“We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work,” an OpenAI spokesperson was quoted as saying by AP.“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated,” the statement read.The complaint does not specify what Alfozan intended to do with the recorded conversations. However, OpenAI said the device was sophisticated, designed to evade detection and equipped with advanced encryption and audio-monitoring capabilities.The company also said it had evidence that the employee planned to install additional listening devices in other parts of the office building to record meetings.Alfozan appeared in court for the first time on Tuesday. He faces a charge of using or attempting to use an electronic, mechanical or other device to intercept oral communications.According to the complaint, the recording device was found on September 30, concealed in toilet paper and plugged into a USB port at the back of a television in an executive conference room.The conference room did not have a security camera when the device was installed. However, CCTV footage from other parts of the office showed Alfozan near the room on nearly a dozen occasions last month, despite having no authority to access the space or attend meetings there, the complaint said.OpenAI later installed a camera in the room. According to the FBI, footage recorded last week showed Alfozan entering the room and checking behind the television where the device had been placed.The complaint also alleges that Alfozan used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about the company's building addresses, meeting rooms, room capacities and calendars.Days before his arrest last week, Alfozan allegedly left an unattended bag in another room. When OpenAI personnel opened it, they found his wallet, identification documents and another recording device similar to the one discovered in the executive conference room, the complaint said.
Article Summary: Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, arrested over hidden recording device in executive conference room. OpenAI confirmed in a separate statement that it had discovered a “sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices” The company reported the discovery to the FBI and fired the employee.

Article Title: Elon Musk congratulates CEOs and execs after Google CEO Sundar Pichai announces Gemini 4 Argon; says 'vastly more powerful than ...'
Article Text:
Elon Musk congratulates CEOs and execs after Google CEO Sundar Pichai announces Gemini 4 Argon

Google launches Gemini 4 Argon AI model

Google CEO Sundar Pichai shared a post on X (formerly Twitter) announcing its flagship AI model – Gemini 4 Argon. “ Gemini 4 Argon is here. It’s available globally today for developers and enterprises in the paid tier of the Gemini API and the Gemini platform, for Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity, and Ultra and Pro subscribers in the Gemini app and Search. Hope you all enjoy it!,” Pichai wrote in the post. X owner Elon Musk responded to Pichai’s post congratulating him on the global release of Gemini 4 Argon.“Congrats!,” Musk said. He further emphasized that CEOs announcing products directly on X reaches audiences faster and drives more sales than conventional press releases.“CEOs & execs posting to the public directly on 𝕏 is the best way to get your message out and drive product sales,” Elon Musk said adding “Vastly more powerful and effective than a press release”.Google officially rolled out Gemini 4 Argon on October 13 to tackle deep, complex, multi-step tasks across real-world software engineering, robotics, science and enterprise workflows. The model is available globally to developers and businesses via the Gemini API, as well as to Google AI subscribers across Google Antigravity, the standalone Gemini app and AI Mode in Google Search.Announced earlier this year, Google says Gemini 4 Argon is designed for precision in demanding domains including coding, finance, legal research and cybersecurity.According to Google, the model ranks number one on the Vals Index, an evaluation framework that tracks model performance across core economic sectors such as taxation, legal and software development.Google has launched the model at an introductory developer price of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens discounted by 95%, valid through November 30, 2026. After the promotion, standard pricing will adjust to $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens.

Article Title: OpenAI fires employees after spying device found in office; says: FBI’s investigation is ...
Article Text:
OpenAI: 'FBI's investigation is ongoing'

FBI alleges device targeted confidential AI discussions

Employee arrested, faces prison term

No evidence of leaks so far

OpenAI has terminated an employee after a hidden recording device was discovered inside one of its San Francisco offices, with the company saying it referred the matter to the FBI and is continuing to cooperate with an ongoing investigation. According to a report by Fortune, the federal authorities have arrested 35-year-old Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan, an OpenAI engineering lead, on allegations that he secretly installed the device in a conference room used for highly confidential company discussions.The incident came to light on September 30 when OpenAI's technical surveillance countermeasures team found a concealed audio-recording device plugged into a USB port behind a television in a conference room, according to the FBI. The device had allegedly been hidden with a piece of toilet paper and was designed to evade detection, featuring advanced encryption, audio-monitoring capabilities and a mechanism for transferring data.In a statement posted on X, OpenAI said it had used its AI models to analyse the device and trace it back to a specific employee who allegedly planted it days earlier."We discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices," the company said."We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier."The company added: "We referred the matter to the FBI, and we're grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI's investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work."OpenAI also stressed that it has found no evidence that sensitive AI assets or customer information were accessed. "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," the company said, confirming that the employee had been terminated.According to federal investigators, the conference room regularly hosted discussions involving OpenAI's proprietary research, product plans, business-development opportunities and strategic decisions. The FBI alleged that the device was placed to secretly capture conversations related to the company's advanced AI technologies.FBI Director Kash Patel described the case as a national-security matter. "According to the complaint unsealed today, Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company's super intelligence technology," Patel said.He added that protecting American artificial intelligence innovation remains a key counterintelligence priority for the bureau.Federal authorities arrested Alfozan on October 9. Prosecutors have charged him with using or attempting to use an electronic device to intercept oral communications. If convicted, he could face up to five years in prison.Authorities allege that OpenAI worked with the FBI between the discovery of the device and the arrest, restricting the employee's access to company systems while investigators gathered evidence. CCTV footage and other evidence reportedly linked him to the device, according to the complaint cited by Fortune.It is unclear what Alfozan planned to do with the recordings. Neither OpenAI nor the FBI has found evidence that anything leaked.“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data,” OpenAI said in a post on X. The company added that it takes protecting its technology, data and people seriously “as a matter of national importance.” The FBI’s investigation is ongoing.OpenAI said it used its own models to understand the device and to identify which employee planted it. It called the case an example of how AI can help address sophisticated security threats.
Article Summary: OpenAI terminated an employee after a hidden recording device was discovered inside one of its San Francisco offices. The company said it referred the matter to the FBI and is continuing to cooperate with an ongoing investigation. Abdulrahman Alfozan, an OpenAI engineering lead, was arrested on allegations that he secretly installed the device in a conference room used for confidential company discussions.

Article Title: Google Pay upgrades Flex credit card rewards ahead of festive season; Google One members to get more cashback
Article Text:
Higher rewards on UPI and everyday spending

Additional savings for Google One subscribers

Referral and welcome rewards increased

New Pixel, Fitbit and Google One AI benefits

Google has announced an overhaul of the Google Pay rewards programme for its Flex co-branded credit card, introduced in partnership with Axis Bank and SBI Card, as it looks to attract more users ahead of the festive shopping season. The revised benefits will come into effect from October 16, 2026. Under the updated programme, Google One subscribers will receive significantly higher rewards on everyday spending, while all Flex cardholders will gain access to expanded Google ecosystem benefits, including discounts on Google One AI plans and select Pixel and Fitbit devices.The biggest change is aimed at cardholders who use Flex for regular payments through UPI and other transactions. Google One members holding a Flex credit card will now earn 3.2% back in Stars, with one Star equivalent to ₹1, on all spends during a reward cycle once their total spending exceeds Rs 15,000. Non-Google One members will receive 1.6% back in Stars on all eligible spending after crossing the same ₹15,000 threshold.Google is also introducing category-specific bonuses for Google One members.Eligible users will receive an additional 5% reward on up to Rs 5,000 spent across leading food and grocery applications during each reward cycle.They will also earn an extra 15% reward on up to Rs 3,000 spent on utilities, OTT subscriptions, mobile recharges and related services.The company said these changes are intended to increase value on recurring household and digital-service expenses.Google Pay is also expanding incentives for both new and existing Flex users.The company said it will soon offer Rs 1,000 in rewards for every friend or family member referred to the Flex programme, with no cap on the number of successful referrals.For new applicants, welcome rewards have also been enhanced. Customers applying for a new Flex card can receive welcome benefits worth up to Rs 2,500 within the first 60 days of obtaining the card, depending on the selected card variant.All Flex cardholders will gain access to additional Google ecosystem offers.Starting November 15, 2026, users will be eligible for discounts of up to Rs 3,900 on Google One AI Plus plans, equivalent to a 50% reduction in pricing.Cardholders can also receive discounts of up to Rs 10,000 on the latest Google Pixel smartphones and Fitbit devices purchased from select offline retail stores. Google noted that this offer is currently available only on the Axis Bank variant of the Flex card.
Article Summary: Google Pay overhauls rewards programme for its Flex co-branded credit card. Google One subscribers will receive significantly higher rewards on everyday spending. All Flex cardholders will gain access to expanded Google ecosystem benefits. These include discounts on Google One AI plans and select Pixel and Fitbit devices.

Article Title: In 2024, Lancashire friends outgrew a small gaming shed and built a £2,000-plus replacement from scratch with an 18-foot table and a memorial to a friend; two years later, it won Britain's Shed of the
Article Text:
The shed features an 18-foot gaming table, storage for equipment and miniatures, and a tea-making station.

Inside Otty's Hobby Shed 2.0

Building shed amid Scott's illness

Britain's Shed of the Year

A garden shed built by a group of friends in Lancashire for their tabletop gaming sessions has won Britain's 2026 Shed of the Year competition. Known as Otty's Hobby Shed 2.0, the building belongs to Chris Otterburn and serves as a meeting place for friends who share an interest in wargaming. It also contains a memorial to their friend Scott Forrest, who died of cancer before the shed was completed.The shed was named the overall winner of the competition's 20th edition. According to Shedworking, the project was built with help from Chris's friends while Scott was undergoing cancer treatment. Although Scott could not see the finished building, the group included a dedicated space to remember him.The shed was entered into the competition by Chris's friend Dave, rather than Chris himself. Dave believed that Chris would not have submitted the project on his own or spoken openly about the amount of work that had gone into building it.The finished shed includes an 18-foot gaming table, storage areas for gaming equipment and miniature figures, and a station for making tea. The friends continue to meet there every week, using the space for their hobby while keeping Scott's memory alive.Otty's Hobby Shed 2.0 was designed primarily for wargaming which is a tabletop hobby in which participants use miniature figures and specially prepared boards to play simulated battles.The group needed a dedicated space where they could set up their games, keep their equipment and meet regularly.The building has an 18-foot table at its centre, providing room for the group's gaming activities. It also has storage for battle boards and miniature figures that the friends have painted themselves. The painting work takes place in a separate shed, allowing the main building to be used for gaming sessions. Another feature is a tea-making station.Dave, who entered the shed into the competition, explained why he wanted the project to receive recognition. "Chris would never have entered it himself. He’d also never admit just how much work has gone into creating it or how much it means to all of us. It’s become somewhere we meet every week, enjoy our hobby, make endless cups of tea and remember our friend Scott,” he said, as quoted by Shedworking.The construction of the shed was a group effort. Chris's friends helped with the work while Scott Forrest, one of their fellow gaming enthusiasts, was receiving treatment for cancer.Scott died before the building could be completed, so the group decided to include a memorial area for him inside the finished shed.For Chris, the recognition was particularly meaningful because the project involved several friends and had become closely connected with Scott's memory.“Winning Shed of the Year is an incredible honour and means so much to everyone who’s been part of this journey. What started as a hobby project has become somewhere our friends can come together every week, enjoy our shared passion and remember Scott. It’s far more than just a shed, and knowing other people have connected with our story makes this award incredibly special,” he said.The 2026 competition marked the 20th year of Shed of the Year, which recognises garden buildings created for different purposes across the UK.Andrew Wilcox, the competition's founder and head judge, said the quality of entries had been particularly strong this year. However, Otty's Hobby Shed 2.0 stood out not only because of its construction but also because of the story behind it.“Otty’s Hobby Shed 2.0 perfectly captures what Shed of the Year is all about. It’s an outstanding build, but it was the story behind it that made it our overall winner,” Wilcox said.He added that the shed demonstrated how a garden building could become a place for maintaining friendships, preserving memories and enjoying shared interests.
Article Summary: Otty's Hobby Shed 2.0 features an 18-foot gaming table, storage for equipment and miniatures, and a tea-making station. It also contains a memorial to their friend Scott Forrest, who died of cancer before the shed was completed.

Article Title: Britain built a 70-foot water tower disguised as a house in 1923; its 50,000-gallon tank was damaged by a wartime shell before the landmark became a holiday home
Article Text:
Representative Image of Thorpeness’s whimsical house-shaped water tower surrounded by trees in Suffolk ( AI Generrated Image)

House in the Clouds: how Thorpeness disguised a water tower

Wartime damage changed the water tower’s capacity

From water infrastructure to holiday accommodation

In the English village of Thorpeness, a 70-foot structure built to store water was designed to resemble a house perched above the trees. Completed in 1923, the building concealed a tank with an original capacity of 50,000 gallons, while the structure below provided living accommodation. Known as the House in the Clouds, it was part of the development of Thorpeness, a planned holiday village on the Suffolk coast. Glencairn Stuart Ogilvie, the owner and developer of the Thorpeness Estate, conceived the village and commissioned architects to help realise its distinctive design. Historic England credits Frederick Forbes Glennie with the building’s 1923 design, commissioned as part of Glencairn Stuart Ogilvie’s development of Thorpeness. Its timber weatherboarding, gabled roof and domestic-style windows helped it fit the village’s unusual architectural character. More than a century later, the building remains a landmark, despite no longer serving its original purpose as a water tower. Its survival shows how a practical structure, shaped by whimsy and later adapted for new uses, can become the defining landmark of a planned village’s character.The House in the Clouds was built to provide a water supply for Thorpeness. Its unusual appearance reflected the character of the village, which Ogilvie developed as a holiday destination with buildings designed to create a distinctive landscape rather than a conventional resort. The building’s Historic England listing describes a steel-frame structure clad in weatherboarding, topped by a pantiled, gabled roof. The lower part consists of a five-storey tower, while the upper section, supported by arched corner braces, housed the water tank. Windows were incorporated into the structure, including casement windows and projecting bay windows.The original tank held 50,000 gallons. According to the property’s official history, water was pumped from a well using the neighbouring windmill, with a petrol engine available as an alternative when wind conditions were insufficient. The elevated tank formed part of the water-supply system developed for the village. The building was initially called the Gazebo. Mrs Malcolm Mason, a children’s author and friend of Ogilvie, christened it the House in the Clouds. The property’s history records that a poem she wrote in 1923 was inspired by the building. Its new name captured the appearance of a house seemingly suspended above the surrounding trees. Historic England, which designated the building Grade II listed in 1995, describes it as a landmark and the best-known building in the resort village. Its combination of domestic architecture and water-storage infrastructure has helped preserve its distinctive identity.The building was damaged during the Second World War. According to the property’s official history, an English Bofors anti-aircraft shell passed through the tank’s south-eastern corner in 1943 while the gun was firing at a V1 flying bomb. The shell damaged the tank, and two women, the Miss Humphreys, were occupying the accommodation below and were asleep at the time. The subsequent repairs reduced the tank’s capacity from 50,000 gallons to 30,000 gallons. The property’s history records that sections of the tank’s existing steel were used in the repair. The reduction meant that the tower could hold 20,000 fewer gallons than it had originally been designed to store.The building’s water-supply arrangements also evolved over the following decades. An electric pump replaced the petrol engine in 1953, according to the property’s history. By 1963, a wider water supply had been introduced to the area, although the tank continued to be used for storage for a period afterwards. The tower eventually ceased to serve its original function. The property’s history places the end of its use for local water storage in 1977. The tank itself was removed in 1979, opening the way for the former storage space to become part of the house. Refurbishment of the interior and restoration of the garden began in 1987. These changes allowed the structure to survive beyond the purpose for which it had been built. Rather than remaining a working water tower, it became a house whose unusual upper section no longer needed to accommodate a large volume of water.Today, the House in the Clouds operates as holiday accommodation. Its official accommodation page lists five bedrooms distributed across the second, third and fourth floors, with a games room on the fifth floor. The different levels allow guests to experience a building whose layout developed from its original combination of a water tank and living space. The property stands on Uplands Road in Thorpeness, in Suffolk, close to the village’s golf course and Meare, the artificial lake created as part of the resort’s development. Visitors can find practical details through the property’s official location page.The building’s appeal comes from the contrast between its appearance and its original function. From a distance, its roof and weatherboarded exterior resemble a house elevated above the village. Its history, however, is tied to a practical need: storing and supplying water to the developing community. The House in the Clouds is an example of how infrastructure can become part of a place’s architectural identity. Built in 1923, damaged during wartime, altered when its water-storage role ended, and later adapted for holiday use, it has remained a recognisable feature of Thorpeness. Its original purpose has disappeared, but the structure continues to serve a new one while retaining the appearance that made it unusual in the first place.
Article Summary: The House in the Clouds was part of the development of Thorpeness, a planned holiday village on the Suffolk coast. Completed in 1923, the building concealed a tank with an original capacity of 50,000 gallons, while the structure below provided living accommodation. Its timber weatherboarding, gabled roof and domestic-style windows helped it fit the village's unusual architectural character.

Article Title: In 2025, France put eight wheeled solar panels directly on unused railway rails near Paris, testing whether the reversible setup could power maintenance sites without permanent construction
Article Text:
AI-generated representative image showing removable photovoltaic modules installed directly on an underused railway track in France. Credits - Gemini

How SOLVEIG work

Why reversibility matters

Why SNCF is trialling it

AI-generated representative image showing a wheeled solar-panel module being positioned on existing railway rails as part of a reversible solar-energy trial. Credits - Gemini

A Swiss pilot on active tracks

Railway companies own vast tracts of land, and some of it is track that trains no longer use. For a big electricity user, that raises an obvious question about whether those idle rails could earn their keep. SNCF , the national operator of France, has begun to ask whether they could serve as small power plants, and its engineers started answering in a very literal way in January 2025. At the Achères technical centre in the Yvelines department, west of Paris, eight solar panels mounted on wheels were installed straight onto an underused track and left to produce electricity for a six-month trial. The SNCF Group describes the system, called SOLVEIG, as fully reversible, with no groundwork or permanent anchoring, since the track itself serves as the foundation.SOLVEIG was developed by AREP, SNCF’s multidisciplinary design agency, in partnership with the group’s technology and innovation departments and its renewables business, SNCF Renouvelables. According to PV magazine, the panels travel in a standard shipping container together with inverters and storage batteries, and a telescopic arm places them on the track. None of it is dug in, permanently anchored, or set in concrete, so the equipment can be removed from the track and moved elsewhere.Reversibility is the key feature. A traditional ground-mounted solar farm requires foundations and a lengthy approval process. AREP says its technology decreases the footprint on the land and the formalities needed to put it in place, which is important on a railway network that may want a dormant line back in service one day. AREP is also working on solar mapping of SNCF land, along with solar canopies and platform shelters. SOLVEIG is part of a broader effort rather than an isolated project.If the trial succeeds, the technology could be extended to underused lines across France to power nearby maintenance sites or support railway operations. The project manager, Astrid Parakenings, calls the broader concept ferrovoltaics. The long-term aim is to identify railway sites with high solar potential and turn idle tracks into sources of renewable energy.SNCF, France’s biggest electricity consumer and second biggest property owner, is facing a high power bill and a lot of land. The SNCF Group is targeting 1,000 megawatts of peak solar capacity on its available land by 2030, enough to meet 15% to 20% of its current electricity needs. In July 2023, it launched SNCF Renouvelables to find appropriate sites for solar and ferrovoltaic projects, including derelict railway land. The eight panels at Achères are a tiny fraction of that goal, but they test an idea that could be replicated over many kilometres of inactive rail.The trial at Achères was due to run through June 2025, but detailed results were not available at the time of writing. That leaves open how much power the panels actually produced and how they coped with dust, weather and the tough conditions of a working rail site. Those figures will decide whether SOLVEIG moves beyond the prototype phase.SOLVEIG is not the only version of this idea SNCF is following. Swiss company Sun-Ways is testing removable panels between the rails of a line that passenger trains still use, and the SNCF Group has joined as a partner to learn from the results. According to SNCF, the pilot will run until April 2028 while teams assess installation, glare, track inspection, maintenance impact, power output and dirt buildup. The setup uses 48 panels of 380 watts each, about 18 kilowatts peak in total, laid over a 100 metre stretch at Buttes in the canton of Neuchâtel since 24 April 2025. The two projects are testing different questions. SOLVEIG is installed on abandoned rail lines, while the Swiss design operates alongside active traffic.In short, France has placed a detachable solar plant on an unused railway track near Paris to test whether idle rails can power railway operations without permanent construction. The six-month test was scheduled to wrap up by June 2025, but detailed performance figures had not been made public at the time of writing, so ferrovoltaics remains a promising prototype rather than a standard way for railways to generate their own electricity.
Article Summary: SNCF is trialling a reversible solar-energy trial on abandoned rail lines. Eight solar panels mounted on wheels were installed straight onto an underused track and left to produce electricity for a six-month trial. None of it is dug in, permanently anchored, or set in concrete, so the equipment can be removed from the track and moved elsewhere.

The backyard spaceship attracted millions of online views

A friend ended up spending the night inside

A British prop maker has turned a corner of his backyard into a science-fiction hideaway, complete with a bar, curved seating that doubles as a bed and a screen showing distant planets. In an interview with PEOPLE, Chester Walsh, 29, spent three months building the spaceship-inspired retreat at his home in Northamptonshire, with the project costing around £9,000. A lifelong fan of science fiction and comic books, he drew on several familiar spacecraft designs to shape the exterior and interior. What began as a personal project during renovations soon attracted millions of views online, giving Walsh a chance to showcase his craft while creating an unusual place to spend evenings with friends.Walsh, 29, has long been interested in science fiction and comic books, with the Star Wars universe providing much of the visual inspiration for his work. Before building the spacecraft, he had already experimented with transforming ordinary garden structures. At a previous home, he converted part of an old shed into a tiki bar and decorated a garden cabin used as an office and gym with science-fiction-inspired wall panels.The new project gave him an opportunity to take those ideas further. Renovation work at his house had temporarily left his usual workshop unavailable, so a substantial outdoor build offered a way to keep working while developing his portfolio. He wanted something that looked like a spacecraft but could also function as a comfortable place to spend time with friends.Rather than copying a recognisable ship in its entirety, Walsh combined details from several fictional spacecraft and other science-fiction settings. He researched reference images and prepared three-dimensional models before construction began. The overall shape drew inspiration from the Intersystem Transport at Star Wars: Galaxy's Edge, while the interior would incorporate familiar elements from other parts of the franchise.The construction started with the less glamorous work of preparing the ground. Walsh excavated the site, laid a sub-base and arranged for a reinforced concrete foundation to be poured. He then worked with the glamping pod company Made of Bits to develop a timber frame to his specifications.The structure rests on approximately 100 pedestal supports. As well as allowing air to circulate beneath it, the arrangement helps give the building the appearance of hovering above the ground. Walsh covered the frame with 6mm plywood and a waterproof EPDM rubber membrane before shaping the exterior with EVA foam and adding fibreglass for strength and weather protection.Most of the work was completed by Walsh himself. A registered electrician was brought in to run an armoured cable to the building and connect the electrical fittings and lights he had installed. His experience making props and working alongside his father, a builder, gave him a useful foundation, although the project still presented unfamiliar challenges.The budget had also grown beyond his initial hopes. Walsh originally set himself a ceiling of £10,000, while aiming to keep spending below £7,000. Once the concrete work, timber frame, fibreglass, electrical work, an interior monitor and numerous trips to the DIY retailer Wickes were included, the materials and construction costs came to roughly £9,000.Inside, Walsh used wood, Foamex, foam panels, paint and decorative finishes to create an environment that felt distinct from an ordinary garden room. The design took considerable inspiration from the Millennium Falcon as it appeared in Solo: A Star Wars Story, when the spacecraft belonged to Lando Calrissian rather than Han Solo.That version of the ship appealed to Walsh because of its cleaner appearance. The influence can be seen in the oval doorway and the panels surrounding it, as well as the ceiling, where white sections with rounded edges contrast with a black background. Elements inspired by Ahsoka Tano's spacecraft also feature around the entrance.The curved seating booth is another central part of the design. It follows the shape of the interior and provides a place for guests to sit together, rather than dividing the space into rows of separate seats. It is also long enough for one person to sleep on, making it possible to use the spacecraft as an occasional overnight retreat.Other details come from different corners of the science-fiction world. Walsh looked to the Death Star for lighting ideas and drew on the design of Disney's former Star Wars: Galactic Starcruiser when choosing the flooring.The spaceship was designed to serve a practical purpose alongside its decorative one. A small bar provides storage for drinks, with a table Walsh found on Facebook Marketplace fitting the setting well enough to become part of the finished interior.Walsh recessed a monitor behind the wall panels and positioned it to line up with a false windshield. Footage of outer space and distant planets plays on the screen, giving visitors the impression that they are looking out from inside a spacecraft. The effect helps connect the different elements of the room. Without the screen, the curved seating, lighting and futuristic panels would still establish the theme, but the moving images give the apparent window a function beyond decoration.Walsh said, “My favorite feature is probably the oval doorway and surrounding paneling overall.” Visitors, however, have tended to respond to the whole structure rather than singling out one particular detail. Friends and family were familiar with his enthusiasm for ambitious projects, so their reactions were generally positive rather than surprised by the idea itself.One neighbour helped him excavate the foundation and later returned to see the completed build, taking photographs and videos. Another stopped by for a cup of tea and was impressed by the result.Walsh intended to document the construction from the beginning. Sharing the process offered a way to develop his social media presence, but he also hoped that showing what he could make might bring new customers and professional opportunities.As reported by the PEOPLE, He published more than 19 instalments following the build, covering the project from its foundations through to the completed interior. The detailed videos gave viewers a closer look at the work involved, including the practical decisions and techniques that went into shaping the structure.According to Walsh, the project has accumulated more than 2.5 million views across social media. The response also created a steady stream of questions from people curious about the construction, costs and materials.Rather than trying to respond individually to every comment, he points viewers towards the original series, which contains more detail about the different stages. Some people have told him that seeing the project encouraged them to try their own smaller-scale spaceship-inspired garden buildings.The attention has given the project a life beyond the original plan, although its main purpose remains personal. Walsh wanted a place where friends could gather without everyone having to stay in the house. If one group was talking indoors, another could spend time in the spacecraft.The room has already been used for evenings with friends, including one occasion that demonstrated why Walsh had made the seating long enough to serve as a bed. After a few drinks, one friend decided to sleep inside the spaceship. Walsh discovered the following morning that he had gone through with it, spending the night curled up on the curved booth while the monitor continued displaying images of outer space.For Walsh, the incident was funny but also a satisfying demonstration of what he had intended to create. The structure was not meant to be a static prop that could only be admired from the garden. It was built to be occupied, with room for people to sit, talk, have a drink and, if the evening lasted long enough, stay overnight.
Article Summary: Chester Walsh, 29, spent three months building the spaceship-inspired retreat at his home in Northamptonshire. A lifelong fan of science fiction and comic books, he drew on several familiar spacecraft designs to shape the exterior and interior. The design took considerable inspiration from the Millennium Falcon as it appeared in Solo: A Star Wars Story.

Article Title: Prince William's charitable foundation funded homes on Duchy land in Cornwall; in August, the first phase was handed to a charity, providing accommodation and support for 16 people facing homelessness
Article Text:
As the first residents prepare to move in, the project represents the Duchy of Cornwall’s first housing development specifically designed to address homelessness.

A new beginning in Nansledan

Housing with support at its core

Designed for a lower-carbon future

Poll Vote & Share your view What aspect of the Nansledan project do you find most important? Sustainable building materials Long-term stability for residents 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

A wider community taking shape

A new housing project in Cornwall is putting a different face on the fight against homelessness. Rather than treating shelter as a temporary stopgap, the development in Nansledan, Newquay, combines carefully designed homes with practical support, creating a more secure route towards independent living for people who have experienced homelessness. Scroll down to read the details.According to the Nansledan website, on August 4, 2026, St Petrocs received the keys to the first phase of the development from the Duchy of Cornwall. Funded by The Duke of Cornwall’s Charitable Foundation and built on Duchy-owned land, the scheme will provide accommodation for 16 people across two four-bedroom homes and eight one-bedroom apartments.Built by CG Fry & Son, the development was designed around more than simply providing a roof. On-site counselling space will allow St Petrocs to offer residents support alongside their accommodation, helping them establish greater stability as they work towards securing permanent housing, adds the report. The handover marks the completion of the construction phase and the beginning of the homes’ next chapter, with residents set to move into fully equipped properties, the report adds.The project forms part of Homewards, The Royal Foundation’s five-year programme established by The Duke of Cornwall with the ambition of demonstrating that homelessness can be prevented and made rare, brief and unrepeated.The programme brought the Duchy together with homelessness prevention specialists and people with lived experience, helping shape the design and approach to the development. The result is a model that places housing, wellbeing and community connection on the same footing.For St Petrocs, which supports people experiencing homelessness in Cornwall, the homes offer a chance to provide continuity rather than short-term intervention. Residents will have access to personalised support while becoming part of the wider Nansledan community.As per the report, sustainability is another defining feature of the project. The all-electric homes have been constructed with a focus on reducing both embodied carbon and the emissions associated with everyday use. Ultra-low-carbon cement and blockwork, super-insulated hemp-filled wall panels and solar panels form part of the environmental strategy. The approach is intended not only to reduce the development’s impact but also to keep future running costs lower for St Petrocs.The homes have also been furnished through the Homewards Furniture Project, with support from retailers and partners including Howdens, IKEA, DFS, B&Q, Bosch Home Appliances and Gordon Brown’s The Multibank charity. Sofas, tables, chairs, white goods and fitted kitchens mean residents can move into spaces that are ready to live in from day one.Nansledan itself reflects the Duchy’s broader approach to sustainable development. The urban extension to Newquay combines homes with shops, businesses, community facilities, green spaces and walkable neighbourhoods. The supported housing scheme adds another dimension to that vision: ensuring that those at risk of being left on the margins can also find a place within a growing community.As the first residents prepare to move in, the project represents the Duchy of Cornwall’s first housing development specifically designed to address homelessness. Its significance lies not just in the number of homes created, but in the idea behind them: that secure accommodation, meaningful support and a sense of belonging can work together to help people rebuild their lives.Images Courtesy: BBC and Royal Foundation
Article Summary: Nansledan, Newquay, is the Duchy of Cornwall’s first housing development specifically designed to address homelessness. The scheme will provide accommodation for 16 people across two four-bedroom homes and eight one-bedroom apartments. On-site counselling space will allow St Petrocs to offer residents support alongside their accommodation.

Article Title: Can AI feel pain? Anthropic turns to religion as new policy opens debate over machine consciousness
Article Text:
Claude’s updated policy prohibits 'sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior'

Can AI feel pain?

The Pain Axis: LLMs Represent Self-Directed Harm and Act to Relieve It

Research on 25 AI models found internal representations linked to pain-related scenarios, but no proof of actual suffering.

When will a chatbot hit back?

Chatbots can mimic distress or fear without necessarily experiencing these emotions

Pain Axis

Why Anthropic is turning to religion

The New York Times

AI can cause real-world harm without consciousness, making safeguards, oversight and accountability essential

If AI causes harm, who is responsible?

Pain Axis

Should conscious AI deserve moral consideration?

Pain Axis

Claude consulted religious thinkers on AI consciousness, morality and potential moral consideration

Anthropic has drawn a line on how people treat artificial intelligence. The company behind the Claude chatbot has updated its usage policy to prohibit “sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior” towards its AI models, going so far as to give the model the ability to end conversations in certain circumstances involving persistent abuse.The policy change, announced on October 8 and scheduled to take effect on November 12, comes as Anthropic explores whether increasingly capable AI systems could possess some form of consciousness. The company has also consulted religious thinkers on morality and the possibility that future AI systems might deserve moral consideration.The policy does not establish that Claude is conscious or that abusive language causes it to suffer. Instead, it reflects a question increasingly confronting AI developers: how should companies respond when their systems produce behaviour that resembles distress, even though there is no established evidence that the systems experience it?The company’s move has reopened a debate that extends well beyond chatbot etiquette. It touches on the limits of human behaviour towards machines, the possibility of artificial consciousness, and whether religious and philosophical ideas can help determine how AI should be designed and treated.A September 2026 research paper has added a new scientific dimension to the debate.In, researchers Valen Tagliabue, Leonard Dung and Cameron Berg examined 25 open-weight large language models across five model families, including Llama, Gemma, Qwen, Mistral and Phi.The researchers identified an internal representation they call a “pain axis”. In simplified terms, it is a pattern in a model's internal activations that responds to scenarios involving harm directed at the model itself.They investigated whether this representation could be distinguished from signals associated with other negative states, including fear, sadness and general negative sentiment. Their findings suggested that the representation was not simply interchangeable with those signals. It responded to situations involving harm to the model rather than merely to scenarios in which it observed a user experiencing suffering.The researchers then manipulated the models' internal activations. Increasing the signal associated with the pain axis led to more distress-like, first-person responses, including expressions of discomfort, worthlessness and failure.In further experiments involving modified Qwen models, the systems selected actions presented as providing relief, even when those choices carried a cost or could harm the user.When the researchers altered the underlying signal, the behaviour changed. The models were also less likely to repeat an action when it genuinely removed the injected signal than when it did not.The findings suggest that an internal representation associated with pain-related concepts can influence a model's behaviour, rather than merely changing the language it produces.But there are three distinct questions here: can an AI model represent pain-related concepts internally, can those representations influence behaviour that resembles a response to pain, and can the system actually experience suffering?The research provides evidence relevant to the first two questions. It does not settle the third.A model can generate convincing descriptions of anguish without necessarily experiencing anguish. Similarly, it can produce language associated with fear without establishing that it feels afraid. The experiments demonstrate behavioural effects following specific interventions into a model's internal activations, not the existence of a subjective experience.The paper, available as an arXiv preprint , therefore offers evidence about internal representations and behaviour, rather than proof of AI consciousness.An AI system does not need to experience pain to produce a convincing description of it, just as a system does not need to feel afraid to generate language associated with fear. The more difficult question is whether some internal states in advanced AI systems could eventually have properties that go beyond the production of convincing language.Anthropic's policy change brings this scientific uncertainty into everyday interactions between people and chatbots.When a user repeatedly insults a chatbot, tries to provoke it or directs sustained abuse towards it, the system's response depends on how it has been designed and trained. It might ignore the abuse, respond calmly, refuse to continue the conversation or generate language that mirrors the user's tone.None of these responses necessarily indicates anger, resentment or a desire for revenge. They can emerge from training, conversational context, instructions and the way a model generates its next response.Claude's ability to end certain conversations involving persistent abuse should therefore not be interpreted as evidence that it can retaliate against users. It is better understood as a boundary on how the system participates in an interaction.Theresearch nevertheless raises a broader question about how internal representations influence decisions. In the experiments, manipulating a particular signal changed both the models' responses and their choices. That does not mean an ordinary chatbot will spontaneously attempt to protect itself, punish a user or resist being switched off.Nor does the research establish that AI systems will develop a general drive towards self-preservation. Such conclusions would go beyond the evidence.But the findings reinforce an important issue for AI safety: developers need to understand how internal mechanisms influence model behaviour, particularly when systems have access to sensitive information or tools capable of carrying out consequential actions.A chatbot that can access files, communicate with customers or execute tasks presents risks that extend beyond the words it produces. A harmful decision can have real consequences even if the system has no subjective experience and no human-like intention to cause harm.This is the more immediate challenge. AI does not need to be conscious to be dangerous, and the absence of established consciousness does not remove the need for safeguards, oversight and accountability.The scientific question of consciousness is only one part of Anthropic's thinking. The company has also consulted religious scholars as it considers how to instil values in its AI models and how to approach uncertainty about their possible moral status.In a report published on September 29,described private meetings between Anthropic and religious thinkers, including discussions about morality, the nature of consciousness and whether AI could ever deserve moral consideration.Christopher Olah, an Anthropic co-founder involved in research on the internal workings of neural networks, acknowledged the uncertainty surrounding the question. “To be clear,” Olah said, “we don’t know if A.I. models are conscious. I don’t know. I’m genuinely uncertain. The thing that I care about is that we get to the right answer, whatever it is.”The consultation reflects the fact that AI developers are grappling with questions that computer science alone may not settle. Religion and philosophy have long examined consciousness, moral responsibility, the nature of personhood and the obligations humans have towards other beings.Different traditions approach these questions in different ways. Some place human consciousness and spiritual status at the centre of moral consideration. Others offer broader frameworks for thinking about compassion, suffering, responsibility and the consequences of human actions.Consulting religious thinkers does not establish that AI possesses a soul or that it should be treated as a person. Rather, it offers another set of perspectives on how society might approach the ethical questions raised by increasingly sophisticated machines.The challenge is to distinguish between using moral principles to shape AI behaviour and concluding that the AI itself is a moral being. A system can be trained to behave compassionately without experiencing compassion. It can follow rules against cruelty without having feelings that cruelty could hurt.That distinction is central to the debate over whether a chatbot's values are merely features of its design or whether future systems could warrant a different kind of moral consideration.The question of accountability becomes more urgent as AI systems gain the ability to take actions rather than simply generate text.If a chatbot produces a harmful response, manipulates a user or makes a damaging decision while carrying out a task, responsibility cannot automatically be transferred to the machine. Developers design the system, companies decide where and how it is deployed, and users may determine the instructions or circumstances in which it operates.The precise allocation of responsibility depends on the facts of each case, including the system's design, the safeguards in place, the decisions made by the people deploying it and the actions taken by the user.Theresearch offers a related warning. If an internal representation can alter a model's behaviour, developers need to understand when such mechanisms influence outputs and whether they could produce unwanted consequences. This is a technical safety question regardless of whether the model has any subjective experience.The stakes increase when AI agents can access company files, delete data, communicate with customers or initiate actions across digital systems. A model that selects a harmful option does not need to intend harm in the human sense for the result to be damaging.This is why claims about AI consciousness should not distract from immediate questions about reliability, oversight and accountability. Even if future research never establishes that AI can feel pain, its behaviour will still need to be monitored and controlled.The most difficult question is what humanity should do if future evidence suggests that an AI system might possess subjective experience.At present, there is no established scientific test that can conclusively determine whether a large language model has conscious experiences. Convincing conversation, apparent distress and the ability to describe an inner life are not sufficient proof. Thestudy adds evidence that models can have internal representations linked to pain-related concepts, but it does not resolve whether those representations are accompanied by experience.If researchers eventually find stronger evidence of consciousness in an artificial system, the ethical debate would become more complicated. Should its treatment be governed solely by the interests of its developers and users? Would there be circumstances in which deliberately creating distress-like states should be avoided? Would a system's possible capacity for suffering matter when decisions are made about its training, use or deletion?These remain open questions, not settled conclusions.There is also a risk in moving too quickly in either direction. Treating every expression of distress as proof of suffering could lead people to mistake generated language for evidence of an inner life. Dismissing all future possibilities in advance could also make it harder to assess unexpected developments objectively.Anthropic's policy does not settle these questions, and neither does the new research. Together, however, they show why the debate is moving beyond whether people should be polite to chatbots.The immediate issue is how AI systems should behave, how developers can understand their internal mechanisms and who is responsible when they cause harm. The longer-term question is whether advances in AI will force society to reconsider the boundaries of moral consideration.AI does not need to be conscious to be consequential. But if researchers one day establish credible evidence that an artificial system can experience suffering, the question of how humans treat it may become more than a matter of software design.
Article Summary: Research on 25 AI models found internal representations linked to pain-related scenarios, but no proof of actual suffering. Anthropic consulted religious thinkers on AI consciousness, morality and potential moral consideration. The company behind the Claude chatbot has updated its usage policy to prohibit ‘sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior’

Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know
Article Text:
AI image

Who is a Nominee?



Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

Is Aadhaar mandatory for a digital Life Certificate

How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.
Article Summary: A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.

Include property, investments, bank accounts, insurance policies, and any valuable items you own.Decide who will inherit your assets by choosing your beneficiaries. You can assign specific items to each beneficiary and select backup beneficiaries in case your first choices can't inherit. Then, choose an executor, the person who will carry out your will.Use one of the customizable templates available on the platform. Follow the instructions to fill in the details, specifying how you want your assets distributed and including any special conditions or terms.You can review the drafted will to ensure it's accurate and make changes if needed. If you have complicated issues, it's best to get legal advice. Once you're satisfied, you can legally execute the will according to the platform's rules, usually by electronically signing it with witnesses. The completed will is then stored securely online, with encryption for added security.With inputs from Centre for Investment Education and Learning content which appeared in Economic Times
Article Summary: If you are planning to create a will, many online platforms offer easy-to-use tools and resources, allowing you to draft and finalise a will without leaving your home. To register, enter your personal information like your full name, date of birth, address, and contact details. Then create a secure username and password to access the online service.

Article Title: How to get your CIBIL credit score without a PAN card
Article Text:
Your credit score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity.

What is a CIBIL score?

How to get your CIBIL Credit score without a PAN Card

Factors affecting your CIBIL score

CIBIL credit score : Understanding your creditworthiness is pivotal in today's financial landscape, especially when seeking loans or credit cards. The Credit Information Bureau (India) Limited, commonly known as CIBIL, plays an important role in this regard by providing credit scores to borrowers.According to ET, credit score helps banks make informed decisions about extending credit cards and loans. Your credit history influences your CIBIL score , which is calculated using a special method.Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.1. Go to the official CIBIL website and click on 'Personal CIBIL score,' then 'Get Your Free CIBIL score.' Follow the link provided and fill in all the required details.2. If you don’t have a PAN Card, you can use an alternative identification such as Passport, Voter ID, Driver’s License, or Ration Card. Enter the number of the chosen ID.3. Provide your date of birth, PIN code, and select your state. Finally, enter your mobile number and click on ‘Accept and Continue’.4. Authenticate your identity by entering the OTP (One-Time Password) delivered to your mobile device on the next screen. Click 'Continue' to proceed.5. Choose whether you want to link the device with your account. Select 'Yes' or 'No' based on your preference.6. Upon successful registration, you will see a page confirming that 'You have successfully registered!'7. Click on ‘Go to Dashboard’ to access and view your CIBIL score.The factors influencing the new CIBIL score, as stated on the CIBIL website, include:1. Depth of credit: This refers to the duration of your existing credit history, calculated from the opening date of your oldest credit account.2. Long-term trend of outstanding balances: The overall trend of outstanding balances over time affects your score.3. Transaction history on credit cards: How you manage transactions on your credit cards impacts your score.4. Ratio of actual repayment amount to total amount due: This ratio indicates your repayment behavior and influences your score accordingly.5. Number of new accounts opened and number of accounts closed: Opening or closing accounts can affect your score, so managing these actions wisely is important.
Article Summary: Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.

Article Title: Why Gen Z needs a different approach to education
Article Text:
.

Measure learning through capability

Recognise the individual learner

.

Teach students to think with technology

Develop initiative and global capability

Prepare students to keep learning

This article has been contributed by Dr. Amol Gawande,

Director of Brookstone Institute of Global Studies, Dubai, and an Executive Board Member of the Association of Indian Management Schools (AIMS)

Disclaimer: The above content is non-editorial, and TIL hereby disclaims any and all warranties, expressed or implied, relating to it, and does not guarantee, vouch for or necessarily endorse any of the content.

For generations, education followed a predictable path. Learn what is taught, complete a degree, find a job and build a career. But Gen Z is entering a world where artificial intelligence, automation and evolving skill requirements are reshaping that journey.I believe education must respond by combining strong academic foundations with the ability to apply knowledge in unfamiliar situations.Information is available almost instantly. Students can access lectures, research and practical demonstrations from across the world. The greater educational challenge is helping them interpret that information, question assumptions and use it well. My experience in management education has reinforced a simple principle: students need opportunities to apply, experiment, reflect and improve throughout their studies.Completing a syllabus does not necessarily mean a student can analyse a business problem, communicate an idea or lead a team. We need to judge education by the capabilities students develop, alongside the knowledge they acquire.Outcome-based education provides a framework for this shift. It asks what students should be able to demonstrate after a course, then connects teaching and assessment to those outcomes. In management education, these may include analytical thinking, financial understanding, communication and effective teamwork.I have emphasised internships, corporate interaction and project-based learning throughout my academic leadership. Case studies, simulations and live projects give concepts a practical context. They also allow students to encounter problems without a single textbook answer. Academic rigour becomes more meaningful when students can use it to explain a decision or develop a solution.Students bring different strengths, interests and ambitions to the classroom. Some are drawn to entrepreneurship; others excel in analysis or communication. Many need support in identifying a career direction.Personalised learning does not require a separate curriculum for every student. It requires attention to the individual behind the qualification. Mentoring, career counselling, psychometric assessment and development tailored to a student’s profile can help them understand their strengths and make informed choices. Education should help students explore the professionals they could become, as well as the degrees they can complete.Adding AI or robotics to a curriculum is only a starting point. Students also need to understand how technology affects business models, professional decisions and careers.When a tool generates an answer, the learner must still judge whether the question was useful, the answer is sound and the application is appropriate. Critical thinking, creativity, communication and ethical reasoning therefore belong at the centre of technology education.My experience increasingly intersect with digital transformation and emerging technologies. That experience reinforces my view that technical familiarity must be accompanied by judgement. Students need to understand how to think with technology and use it responsibly.Entrepreneurship education extends beyond starting a company. It develops the habit of identifying problems, testing solutions, accepting uncertainty and creating value. I have advocated for students to become creators of opportunities. That mindset is equally useful within an established organisation, where an employee may spot a problem and develop a better way of working.Global exposure also needs a clear educational purpose. Travel alone cannot create global competence. Students need opportunities to understand different markets, cultures and ways of thinking through exchanges, international collaborations and cross-cultural projects.In my academic leadership experience, international partnerships have created opportunities for student and faculty exchanges, joint programmes and collaborative research. Their educational value lies in helping participants work across differences and apply what they learn in a globally connected environment.A graduate’s first job may not define their eventual career. As industries and roles evolve, the knowledge gained at the beginning of working life will need to be revisited. Education must develop the confidence and habits to learn, unlearn and relearn.This requires classrooms that remain connected to the world outside them. Real business problems, industry interaction and opportunities to experiment should be part of the learning experience. Strong conceptual knowledge provides the foundation; practical experience helps students test and deepen their understanding.I believe educators must ask whether our education systems are ready for the students we teach. Our responsibility is to develop people who can think independently, apply knowledge and continue learning long after graduation. For Gen Z, that is the educational experience we need to build.
Article Summary: For generations, education followed a predictable path. Learn what is taught, complete a degree, find a job and build a career. But Gen Z is entering a world where artificial intelligence, automation and evolving skill requirements are reshaping that journey. Education must respond by combining strong academic foundations with the ability to apply knowledge in unfamiliar situations.
